qarun.title: Qarun: “I was only given it because of knowledge I have”
participants: His people from the Children of Israel
qarun.eventDescription: Qarun was from the people of Musa, and Allah gave him treasures whose keys would burden a band of strong men. His people advised him: Do not exult arrogantly; seek the Hereafter through what Allah has given you, do not forget your share of this world, and do good as Allah has done good to you. He said: “I was only given it because of knowledge I have.” He went out before his people in his adornment, and those who desired worldly life wished: “Oh, would that we had like what was given to Qarun! He is one of great fortune.” But those given knowledge said: “Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better.” Allah caused the earth to swallow him and his home, and those who had wished for his position the day before began to say: Had Allah not been gracious to us, He would have made the earth swallow us.
qarun.historicalContext: In Surah al-Qasas, within the story of Musa and his people.
qarun.problemType: Arrogance over success and wealth and attributing it to oneself, or being dazzled by what others have and feeling inferior
qarun.responseType: Attributing blessings to Allah, doing good with them, and looking at outcomes rather than appearances
principles: A blessing is a test, and attributing it to one's cleverness alone is the beginning of tyranny
Doing good with a blessing is its practical gratitude
Outward appearance does not reveal the outcome; do not judge by glitter
True knowledge protects from being dazzled by worldly adornment
modernApplications: When you succeed at work or study, say: this is from my Lord's favour — and mention those who helped you
Follow fewer accounts that show off wealth if they fill you with discontent
Set aside a fixed part of your income for doing good; it applies “do good as Allah has done good to you”
In worldly matters look at those below you, and in religious matters at those above
notToApplyTo: The story does not condemn wealth or seeking provision, but arrogance, forgetting the Giver, and corruption
behaviorObservations: Qarun was advised gently and in a balanced way: do not forget your share of this world
Those who wished judged by appearance; people of knowledge judged by outcome
The wishers changed their minds in a single day
whatToAvoid: Attributing success to yourself alone
Building your contentment on what others own
qarun.reflection: If you saw the outcome of what you wish you had from others, you might praise Allah for what you have.

sulayman-naml.title: Sulayman and the ant: “My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favour”
sulayman-naml.eventDescription: Sulayman marched with his soldiers of jinn, men and birds. When they came to the valley of the ants, an ant said: “O ants, enter your dwellings so that Sulayman and his soldiers do not crush you while they perceive not.” He smiled, amused at her words; he did not look down on the words of a tiny creature, but turned to his Lord in gratitude: “My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents.” And when the throne of the Queen of Sheba was brought to him in the blink of an eye, he said: “This is from the favour of my Lord to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful.”
sulayman-naml.historicalContext: In Surah al-Naml. Sulayman was given a kingdom such as no one after him would have.
sulayman-naml.problemType: How to handle success, promotion and blessings without changing yourself or forgetting the weak
sulayman-naml.responseType: Gratitude with the heart, the tongue and good deeds, and attention to those weaker
principles: A blessing is a test just as a calamity is
Gratitude is through good deeds, not the tongue alone
One sign of balanced strength is paying attention to the voice of the weak
Remembering the blessing of one's parents is part of complete gratitude
modernApplications: With every success or promotion say: “This is from my Lord's favour to test me,” and pair it with charity or a good deed
If you become responsible for others, listen to the weakest people on your team
Each night write down three small blessings you had that day
Mention your parents' part in your success, and pray for them
notToApplyTo: Gratitude does not mean denying your effort or belittling yourself, but attributing both effort and success to Allah
behaviorObservations: He smiled at the ant's words and did not dismiss them
He immediately turned the moment into supplication and gratitude
He mentioned his parents in his blessing
whatToAvoid: Forgetting the Giver at the moment of success
Belittling the weak or insignificant
sulayman-naml.reflection: Every blessing that reaches you carries a hidden question: will I be grateful or ungrateful? Your answer is what you do with it.

sahib-jannatayn.title: The owner of the two gardens: “What Allah willed; there is no power except in Allah”
participants: The owner of the two gardens
sahib-jannatayn.eventDescription: Allah gave a man two gardens of grapevines bordered with palm trees, with crops between them. He said to his companion while boasting in conversation: “I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men.” He entered his garden and said: “I do not think this will ever perish.” His companion advised him: “And why did you not say, when you entered your garden, ‘What Allah willed; there is no power except in Allah’?” His fruits were destroyed, and he began turning his hands over in regret for what he had spent on it, while it had collapsed upon its trellises.
sahib-jannatayn.historicalContext: A parable Allah gave in Surah al-Kahf, the surah it is recommended to recite on Fridays.
sahib-jannatayn.problemType: Boasting about wealth, children or achievements, or fearing the loss of blessings and the evil eye
sahib-jannatayn.responseType: Remembering Allah when seeing a blessing, attributing it to Him, and leaving boasting
principles: “What Allah willed; there is no power except in Allah” is a fortress for the blessing and the heart
Boasting before people breaks their hearts and exposes the blessing to loss
A righteous companion advises you even if he has less wealth
Nothing in this world lasts except what is done for Allah's sake
modernApplications: Make “Ma sha' Allah, la quwwata illa billah” a habit whenever you see something you admire in yourself, your family or your wealth
Do not post every detail of your blessings in front of those suffering their loss
If you have less than a friend who boasts, advise him gently as his companion did, and do not belittle yourself
Spend from your blessing before a day comes when you “turn your hands over” in regret
notToApplyTo: Not every loss of blessing is a punishment; trials also befall the righteous to raise them
behaviorObservations: The believing companion neither envied nor stayed silent, but advised
He tied his advice to an easy, practical phrase
The owner of the gardens only learned after the loss
whatToAvoid: Boasting about wealth and children before people
Thinking the blessing lasts by your effort alone
sahib-jannatayn.reflection: One phrase at the door of your blessing may protect it: What Allah willed; there is no power except in Allah.

yusuf-muraawada.title: Yusuf and the minister's wife: “I seek refuge in Allah” and “Prison is dearer to me”
subCategories: Holding to principle at a cost
yusuf-muraawada.eventDescription: Yusuf was a young stranger in the house of al-‘Aziz. The woman in whose house he lived sought to seduce him; she closed the doors and said: Come to me. He said: “I seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, he is my master, who has made good my residence. Indeed, wrongdoers will not succeed,” and ran for the door. Then the pressure grew when the women of the city joined in their scheming and he was threatened with prison, and he chose prison over sin: “My Lord, prison is dearer to me than that to which they invite me. And if You do not avert from me their plan, I might incline toward them and be of the ignorant.”
yusuf-muraawada.historicalContext: In Surah Yusuf, after he was sold as a slave in Egypt and before his imprisonment.
yusuf-muraawada.problemType: Forbidden temptation at work, in study or in relationships, with pressure from others that may cost you if you refuse
yusuf-muraawada.responseType: Seeking refuge in Allah, physically leaving the place, asking for help, and accepting worldly loss to protect one's faith
emotionsAddressed: Fear of loss if you refuse
principles: Fleeing the place of temptation is strength, not cowardice
Loyalty to those who were good to you is a motive for chastity
Do not trust your own strength alone; ask Allah to turn it away from you
A worldly loss with a pure heart is dearer than a gain with sin
modernApplications: If a relationship or conversation is dragging you towards the forbidden, close the door now: delete, block, change place
Do not be alone with someone you fear temptation with at work or study
If you are threatened with losing a job or opportunity unless you compromise your principles, seek advice and look for an alternative; Allah compensates
Pray sincerely: “If You do not avert their plan from me, I might incline toward them”; admitting weakness before Allah is strength
notToApplyTo: If there is harassment or blackmail at work, the story does not mean staying silent; document it and report to the relevant authorities
behaviorObservations: He said “I seek refuge in Allah” at once, without negotiating with the idea
He physically moved towards the door
He consciously chose prison and asked Allah for help
whatToAvoid: Staying in the place of temptation claiming you can resist
Taking the small first steps lightly
yusuf-muraawada.reflection: Sometimes the prison you choose for Allah's sake is the road to an empowerment you never imagined.

nuh-ibnih.title: Nuh and his son: “O my son, come aboard with us”
subCategories: A child who drifts from the parents' way
nuh-ibnih.eventDescription: Nuh called his people for centuries. When the flood came, he called to his son, who was apart: “O my son, come aboard with us and be not with the disbelievers.” The son said: “I will take refuge on a mountain to protect me from the water.” He said: “There is no protector today from the decree of Allah, except for whom He gives mercy,” and the waves came between them and he was among the drowned. Nuh called to his Lord: “My Lord, indeed my son is of my family.” When Allah made the matter clear to him, he said: “My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking that of which I have no knowledge. And unless You forgive me and have mercy upon me, I will be among the losers.”
nuh-ibnih.historicalContext: In Surah Hud. Nuh was one of the messengers of firm resolve, yet his son was not guided.
nuh-ibnih.problemType: A son or daughter who has drifted from the religion or the family's values despite every effort, with the parent blaming themselves
nuh-ibnih.responseType: Continuing to call with love until the last moment, while accepting that guidance is in Allah's hands
principles: A parent's righteousness does not guarantee the child's; do not punish yourself
Calling with love (“O my son”) remains even in the deepest disagreement
Guidance is from Allah; yours are the means and the supplication
Trusting in material means alone (“I will take refuge on a mountain”) is an illusion
modernApplications: If your child drifts from prayer or values, do not cut the rope of love; keep inviting gently and praying
Stop punishing yourself with “Where did I go wrong?” if you have taken the means
Keep a regular supplication for your child in your prostration
Consult a parenting specialist if the drifting comes with danger (addiction, bad company)
notToApplyTo: The story does not mean abandoning upbringing and follow-up on the grounds that guidance is in Allah's hands
behaviorObservations: He called his son with a term of affection at the hardest moment
He did not stop inviting despite his son's refusal
He submitted to Allah's command and sought forgiveness when it was made clear
whatToAvoid: Endless self-punishment
Cutting off the child who has drifted
nuh-ibnih.reflection: A prophet of firm resolve whose son was not guided; let your heart rest: your task is to call with love, and guidance is in Allah's hands.

luqman-wasaya.title: Luqman's advice to his son: “O my son”
luqman-wasaya.eventDescription: Luqman gave his son comprehensive advice, beginning each time with “O my son”: he forbade him from associating partners with Allah, for it is a great injustice; taught him that Allah sees the small and the great; commanded him to pray, enjoin good and be patient with what befalls him; forbade him from arrogance towards people: “Do not turn your cheek in contempt toward people and do not walk through the earth exultantly”; and taught him manners of walking and speaking: “Be moderate in your pace and lower your voice.”
luqman-wasaya.historicalContext: In Surah Luqman; between the pieces of advice comes Allah's command to honour parents even if they call to associating partners with Him.
luqman-wasaya.problemType: How to advise your son or daughter without driving them away, and what to focus on in upbringing
luqman-wasaya.responseType: Advising with affection and giving reasons, combining belief, worship and character
principles: “O my son”: advice begins with the relationship before the information
Give the reason with the command: “Indeed, association is great injustice”
Order the priorities: foundations before details
Character with people is an essential part of religious upbringing
modernApplications: Choose a calm time for advice, not a moment of anger or in front of others
Replace “do it because I said so” with explaining the reason in language your child understands
Do not flood your child with dozens of orders; choose the three most important things this month
Teach humility and a lowered voice by example before words
notToApplyTo: Preaching alone is not enough if example and a warm relationship are missing
behaviorObservations: He repeated “O my son” in every piece of advice
He gave the reason with the ruling
He combined belief, worship, character and daily manners
whatToAvoid: Advising by shouting or belittling
Focusing on appearances and neglecting character
luqman-wasaya.reflection: Before telling your child what to do, make sure they hear in your voice: O my son.

adam-iblis.title: Adam and Iblis: “Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves” and “I am better than him”
adam-iblis.eventDescription: Iblis erred when commanded to prostrate: he refused and said, “I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay” — justifying his disobedience through comparison and arrogance, and never admitting it. Adam and Hawwa' erred when they ate from the tree, and they said at once: “Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers.” Adam received words from his Lord, and He accepted his repentance. Two mistakes, two paths: admission saved Adam, arrogance destroyed Iblis.
adam-iblis.historicalContext: In Surahs al-A‘raf and al-Baqarah. The first mistake and the first repentance in human history.
adam-iblis.problemType: You made a mistake and feel inclined to justify it or blame others, or fear your mistake will not be forgiven
adam-iblis.responseType: A clear admission without justification, asking for forgiveness, and learning from the mistake
principles: A mistake is not the end of the road; persistence and justification are the danger
Arrogance turns a small mistake into ruin
Admitting “I wronged myself” is the first door of repentance
Comparing yourself with others (“I am better than him”) is the fuel of arrogance
modernApplications: When you wrong someone, begin your apology with “I was wrong” — without “but”
Watch your inner voice: do you justify your mistakes by comparing yourself with others?
Memorise Adam's supplication and repeat it after every sin
Make the mistake a lesson, not an identity: “I made a mistake” does not mean “I am bad”
notToApplyTo: Admitting before Allah does not mean exposing yourself before people for sins Allah has concealed
behaviorObservations: Adam and Hawwa' admitted at once: “We have wronged ourselves”
Iblis offered an outwardly logical argument to justify his disobedience
Allah taught Adam the words by which to repent
whatToAvoid: A conditional apology (“sorry, but…”)
Justifying the mistake because others are worse
adam-iblis.reflection: The difference between Adam and Iblis is not that one never erred, but that one said: I wronged myself.

zakariya-dua.title: Zakariyya: “And never have I been unblessed in my supplication to You, my Lord”
zakariya-dua.eventDescription: Zakariyya grew so old that his bones weakened and his head was full of white hair, and his wife was barren. Yet he called his Lord in a private call, and reminded himself of his history with Allah: “And never have I been unblessed in my supplication to You, my Lord” — You have never disappointed me. Allah gave him glad tidings of Yahya. He marvelled given the means, and was told: “It is easy for Me, for I created you before, while you were nothing.” Allah praised him and his family: “Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds and supplicate Us in hope and fear.”
zakariya-dua.historicalContext: In Surahs Maryam, al-Anbiya' and Al ‘Imran. His supplication came after he saw Allah's provision reaching Maryam in the sanctuary.
zakariya-dua.problemType: Delay in having children or marrying, or a long-awaited wish whose means seem impossible
zakariya-dua.responseType: Continuing to pray with certainty, together with contentment and hastening to good deeds
emotionsAddressed: Despair of the wish coming true
principles: What is impossible in your means is not impossible for Allah
Remember your history with Allah: how many times has He answered you?
A private supplication is closer to sincerity
Do not be impatient for the answer and abandon supplication
modernApplications: Write a list of times Allah answered your prayers; it is your own “never have I been unblessed in my supplication”

Hasten to do good for others while you wait for what you hope for

notToApplyTo: Not every supplication is answered with exactly what was asked; harm may be averted or reward stored, and contentment is part of faith
behaviorObservations: He prayed in a hidden voice

He ended his supplication with contentment: “and You are the best of inheritors”
whatToAvoid: Giving up supplication because the wait is long

zakariya-dua.reflection: Before you say “impossible”, remember how many times you said “O Lord” and He did not disappoint you.

musa-khidr.title: Musa and al-Khidr: “May I follow you so that you teach me some of the right guidance you have been taught?”
subCategories: Patience with what you do not understand
musa-khidr.eventDescription: Musa was asked: Who is the most knowledgeable of people? He said: I am. Allah reproached him for not attributing knowledge to Him, and told him He had a servant more knowledgeable than him. So Musa — a prophet to whom Allah spoke — travelled seeking knowledge, and said to al-Khidr courteously: “May I follow you on condition that you teach me from what you have been taught of sound judgement?” He saw things that appeared evil: a ship holed, a boy killed, and a wall rebuilt for miserly people — and he could not stay patient. Then al-Khidr revealed the wisdom: the ship was damaged so it would escape a king who seized every ship; the boy would have burdened his parents; and under the wall was a treasure for two orphans.
musa-khidr.historicalContext: In Surah al-Kahf, with details of the beginning of the story in al-Bukhari and Muslim.
musa-khidr.problemType: Difficulty in study or learning, or distress at a decree whose wisdom you cannot see (a loss, a delay, a closed door)
musa-khidr.responseType: Humility and patience in learning, and trust that there is wisdom behind decrees that we cannot see
principles: Seeking knowledge never stops, however far you have come
Humility is a condition of learning
What you see as evil may be protection from a greater evil
Patience in learning is harder than learning itself
modernApplications: If study feels hard, remember that a prophet travelled and tired himself to learn; the effort is part of the road
Ask your teacher or a top-performing classmate humbly and without embarrassment
If a door closes before you (an admission, a job, an opportunity), say: perhaps it is a ship holed so that it would be saved
Do not judge an event on its day; wait until the picture is complete
notToApplyTo: al-Khidr's actions were by special revelation and cannot be imitated; no one may harm people claiming hidden wisdom
behaviorObservations: A prophet to whom Allah spoke travelled to learn from someone else
He apologised every time he forgot the condition of patience
He learned that the outward appearance of events may differ from their inner reality
whatToAvoid: Judging events hastily
Being arrogant about what you know
musa-khidr.reflection: Perhaps the door that closed in your face was a ship holed so that it would be saved.

abasa.title: “He frowned and turned away”: do not let the important distract you from the weak
abasa.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ was busy inviting some notables of Quraysh, hoping they would accept Islam, when ‘Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum — who was blind — came saying: Teach me from what Allah has taught you. The Prophet ﷺ frowned and turned away from him. The Quran was revealed reproaching him: “He frowned and turned away because there came to him the blind man. But what would make you perceive, O Muhammad, that perhaps he might be purified?” After that the Prophet ﷺ honoured him, and appointed him to govern Madinah during some of his expeditions.
abasa.historicalContext: In Makkah. Al-Tirmidhi narrated from ‘A'ishah that the surah was revealed about Ibn Umm Maktum.
abasa.problemType: Being busy with people of status and wealth at the expense of ordinary people, or being the one neglected because you are “not important”
abasa.responseType: Giving each person their due attention according to their sincerity, not their status, and accepting correction
principles: Do not measure people by their social status
The one sincere in seeking deserves your time more
Accepting reproach and correcting course is part of a complete character
Even facial expressions are a responsibility, even if the other person cannot see them
modernApplications: At work: do you attend to the big client and neglect the small one? Reorder your attention
In a gathering: give the poor, the young and the weak the same attention you give the notable
If you are neglected because you are “not important”, know that Allah revealed Quran about a man like you
If someone points out a mistake in how you treat people, admit it and put it right, as the Prophet ﷺ honoured Ibn Umm Maktum afterwards
notToApplyTo: The verse does not forbid setting priorities at work, but forbids basing them on status and wealth
behaviorObservations: His intention was good (inviting the notables), yet he was reproached
He accepted the reproach and changed his behaviour
He raised the standing of the man he had turned away from
whatToAvoid: Justifying neglect of the weak by good intentions
Measuring people by their usefulness to you
abasa.reflection: Allah revealed verses recited until the Day of Resurrection for the sake of a blind man turned away from for a moment; never belittle anyone.
